name: Megan Rossi
who: RD, PhD (King's College London); founder and director of The Gut Health Clinic (London and Manchester) and research fellow at King's.
why: Runs a real gut-health clinic and an active research fellowship at the same time, with published work (50+ papers) underpinning a large public-education platform.
takeaway: Treat gut symptoms with a real clinical plan, not with a generic wellness gut-health trend.

name: Emily Leeming
who: RD, PhD; nutrition scientist at King's College London, author of Genius Gut (2024).
why: Translates King's/ZOE gut-microbiome cohort research into clinical dietetic guidance, a newer but credentialed voice in the gut-health space.
takeaway: Pay attention to fiber and plant-food diversity as daily inputs to your gut microbiome.

name: Will Bulsiewicz
who: MD; dual board-certified in internal medicine and gastroenterology; US Medical Director at ZOE personalized-nutrition platform.
why: A practicing GI physician, not a self-taught influencer, whose Fiber Fueled work reset mainstream fiber and gut-health messaging at mass scale.
takeaway: Build meals around fiber-rich plants first, to feed the gut microbes that keep you healthy.

name: Kelly Jones
who: RD, CSSD; sports dietitian in private practice (Student Athlete Nutrition), regular contributor to Runner's World and other outlets.
why: Working clinical sports dietitian whose one-on-one athlete practice feeds a long-running national nutrition-journalism byline.
takeaway: Pair sports-nutrition articles you read with an actual one-on-one consult before making big changes.

name: Yasi Ansari
who: MS, RDN, CSSD; sports dietitian for UCLA Athletics and national media spokesperson for the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.
why: Practices with Division I athletes while serving as the profession's own national voice in mainstream media.
takeaway: Treat athlete nutrition as a coached, individualized plan, not generic eat-more-protein advice.

name: Leslie Bonci
who: MPH, RDN, CSSD, LDN; sports-nutrition consultant, past dietitian for the Pittsburgh Steelers and Kansas City Chiefs, current consultant to Carnegie Mellon athletics and Pittsburgh Ballet Theatre.
why: One of the longest-serving, most credentialed pro-team sports dietitians in the US, still actively consulting for elite teams and performing-arts companies decades in.
takeaway: Adapt your fueling plan to the specific physical demands of your sport or performance art.

name: Cynthia Sass
who: MPH, MA, RD, CSSD; performance dietitian who has consulted for the New York Yankees and other pro athletes; longtime Health magazine contributing nutrition editor.
why: A rare RD with genuine pro-sports clinical credentials paired with a two-decade national media platform.
takeaway: Apply pro-athlete attention to recovery nutrition, like eating within a defined post-workout window.

name: Jill Castle
who: MS, RDN; pediatric dietitian in private practice (Jill Castle Nutrition), author of six children's-nutrition books, host of The Nourished Child podcast.
why: Over 30 years translating hands-on pediatric feeding-practice work into parent-facing guidance and clinical training.
takeaway: Let your child decide how much to eat from what you offer, not every bite.

name: Jennifer Anderson
who: RD, MS in public health (Johns Hopkins); founder of Kids Eat in Color and CEO of BetterBites, digital feeding-therapy programs for families.
why: Runs an actual clinical treatment platform for picky eating and feeding challenges while building one of the largest pediatric-feeding audiences among credentialed dietitians.
takeaway: Use structured, repeated food exposure rather than pressure or bribery for a picky eater.

name: Sarah Remmer
who: RD; Alberta-based pediatric and prenatal dietitian in private practice, author and parenting-nutrition writer.
why: A leading Canadian clinical voice on infant, toddler and prenatal feeding, working one-on-one with families alongside her writing.
takeaway: Seek dietitian guidance during pregnancy and infant feeding rather than relying on generic online advice.

name: Brenda Davis
who: RD; plant-based nutrition specialist and author who has led diabetes-nutrition programs with the Pima Nation and in the Marshall Islands.
why: Among the most credentialed, longest-standing plant-based dietitians, with population-level clinical program results behind the books.
takeaway: Use a well-planned plant-based diet as a tool for diabetes prevention and management.

name: Vesanto Melina
who: RD; co-author with Brenda Davis of foundational plant-based nutrition texts (Becoming Vegan, Becoming Raw) and a longtime plant-based dietetics educator.
why: Co-wrote reference texts that clinical plant-based dietetic practice still draws on today.
takeaway: Plan a plant-based diet deliberately around B12, iron, and protein, not just by removing meat.

name: Kate Scarlata
who: MPH, RDN; Boston-based digestive-health dietitian specializing in IBS, SIBO and low-FODMAP care; co-author of The Complete Low-FODMAP Diet.
why: The clinical dietitian most associated with bringing the Monash low-FODMAP research into mainstream IBS care, with 30+ years in digestive-health practice.
takeaway: Work with a dietitian to trial a structured low-FODMAP elimination and reintroduction for digestive symptoms.

name: Evelyn Tribole
who: MS, RDN; co-creator of the Intuitive Eating framework, trainer of over 2,600 certified counselors worldwide, international speaker.
why: Co-authored the book that defined an entire clinical counseling approach now certified and practiced globally.
takeaway: Practice one meal a week with no rules and full attention — relearn hunger and fullness.

name: Elyse Resch
who: MS, RDN, CEDS-S; co-creator of Intuitive Eating, eating-disorder specialist with over 40 years in private practice.
why: The clinical-practice half of the Intuitive Eating partnership, still seeing clients and training eating-disorder specialists.
takeaway: Practice eating without external food rules and relearn your own hunger and fullness signals.

name: Angie Asche
who: RD, CSSD; founder of Eleat Sports Nutrition, working with collegiate and endurance athletes, author of Chase the Podium.
why: Runs a visible independent sports-dietitian practice and extends its clinical fueling work into published athlete-nutrition education.
takeaway: Treat fueling for a big event like a race as its own planned project, not routine eating.

name: Kelly Pritchett
who: PhD, RD, CSSD; sports-nutrition professor at Central Washington University and team dietitian consultant.
why: Combines an academic research role with hands-on team consulting, representative of the researcher-practitioner track in sports dietetics.
takeaway: Look for sports-nutrition advice from someone who both researches the science and coaches real teams.

name: Toby Smithson
who: MS, RDN, CDCES; diabetes lifestyle specialist, founder of DiabetesEveryDay, author of Diabetes Meal Planning and Nutrition for Dummies.
why: One of the most established diabetes-specialist dietitians, bridging one-on-one CDCES clinical counseling with widely used patient education.
takeaway: Use structured diabetes meal-planning support from a certified diabetes educator rather than improvising.
